summary.value: The article proposes an altered Weisfeiler-Lehman approach that operates on the edges instead of nodes. Based on this, the authors design a new GNN architecture. The article discusses the expressive power by showing that EB-1WL lies between 1-WL and 2-WL. More precisely, they provide a lower bound using homomorphism counts from the class of treewidth-2 chordal graphs. Furthermore, the authors provide a first-order-logic equivalent formulation. Finally, an experimental evaluation shows a favourable performance of their GNN architecture on graph classification and edge-level tasks.

strengths.value:
1. The article is easy to follow
2. EB-1WL gains expressivity over NC-1WL with a quite simple tweak
3. EB-1WL achieves good results on the QM9 dataset

weaknesses.value:
1. The novelty is limited. The authors propose only a slight alteration of the NC-1WL method. 
2. The expressivity discussion is limited. While the authors formulate some lower bound (Thm.5), the experimental results on e.g. BREC are not put into perspective. It is unclear what the increased expressivity can be actually attributed to. 
3. It is unclear what the role of the first-order-logic formulation is. I don't see any implications of this. 
4. While the authors' approach is based on NC-1WL, it is never compared to in Section 6. 
5. Table 1 contains only very few competitor methods. It would be interesting to compare to the methods from Table 4 on synthetic datasets as well. 
6. Theorem 3 is incomplete. The second sentence is not a consequence of the first.  
7. Lines 178-181 need to be explained in more detail. While the Chiba&Nishizeki algorithm is even mentioned in the abstract, it is never discussed. I would recommend to at least mention what the arboricity is. Otherwise, Proposition 1 is not understandable.

questions.value:
1. How does EB-1WL compare to ordinary 1-WL on graphs where nodes AND edges have triangle count features? 
2. Concerning W3 above: Are there any implications of the first-order-logic formulation?
3. On molecular graphs, expressivity beyond 1-WL is rarely needed. How do you explain the performance improvements? 
4. Can some of the experimental results be explained by Theorem 5?
5. Theorem 3 is proven using two CSL graphs (though with 16 nodes). Do you have an intuition why in Table 1 the CSL results for EB-GNN do not improve over MPNN+C3?

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission4539 by Reviewer L5Lp

comment.value:
Thank you for reviewing our paper and for engaging in the rebuttal.

> Q1 How does EB-1WL compare to ordinary 1-WL on graphs where nodes AND edges have triangle count features?

It is easy to see that EB-1WL can simulate the 1-WL test where both nodes and edges have triangle counts (indeed, every edge receives the number of triangles it belongs to after the first iteration; then, every node can be assigned the number of triangles it belongs to by summing the number of triangles of its edges, using Equations (2) and (4)). On the other hand, in the BREC dataset we have found an example of two graphs that cannot be distinguished by 1-WL where both nodes and edges have triangle counts but can be with EB-1WL. We have added the example and additional discussion in Appendix E of our revised paper.

>Q2 Concerning W3 above: Are there any implications of the first-order-logic formulation?

We believe this is best answered together with Question 4 regarding Theorem 5. We believe that our answer for Q4 also covers this question.

> Q3: On molecular graphs, expressivity beyond 1-WL is rarely needed. How do you explain the performance improvements?

It is true that most molecular graphs are pairwise distinguishable (see for example 1-WL Expressiveness Is (Almost) All You Need; Zopf; IJCNN 2022). However, molecular properties are often connected to cyclic structures in the graph. While the MPNN might be able to distinguish all molecules in the graph, they are still unable to solve certain tasks directly (for example they cannot count cycles: see Can graph neural networks count substructures?; Chen at al., NeurIPS 2020) which can influence their predictive performance. By increasing the expressivity, we allow the GNN to solve certain tasks directly, thus boosting their predictive performance and ability to generalize.

>Q4: Can some of the experimental results be explained by Theorem 5?

Yes, we believe that Theorem 5 (and Theorem 4) provides significant insight into the practical performance. In concrete terms, in BREC where the effect is easiest to see, we have briefly analysed what motifs distinguish those graphs that are equivalent under triangle counts. An example of a treewidth 2 chordal graph $P$ that distinguishes most graphs even when their triangle counts are the same is the graph $G = (V, E), V = \\{1,2,3,4\\}, E = \\{\\{1,2\\},\\{2,3\\},\\{3,4\\}, \\{4,1\\}, \\{1,3\\}\\}$  (a rectangle with 1 diagonal).

Beyond simple distinguishability in BREC, recent expressivity research has identified the theoretical capabilities of GNNs regarding homomorphism counting as highly relevant for practice. At a high-level the reasoning behind this is that this is tightly coupled to the ability of the GNN to actually compute the homomorphism counts and related graph properties (cf., Jin et al. ICML 2024, Lanzinger and Barceló ICLR 2024, Zhang et al. ICLR 2024) rather than just creating different embeddings without deeper meaning.

We would also like to note that while there is significant work on injecting various specific patterns into GNN architectures, to the best of our knowledge such chordal cycles like $P$ have not been used in the literature. Since our architecture is fundamentally strong enough to capture such patterns (illustrated by Theorem 5), it does not rely on user-choice and intuition of what powerful patterns are, but enables the architecture to learn such features by itself.

Regarding Q2, the value of the logical characterisation is along the exact same lines as Theorem 5. It gives us a deep understanding not only of distinguishing graphs, but what kinds of functions and features can be learned by the GNN. The analogous characterisation of 1WL in terms of graded modal logic (Logical Expressiveness of Graph Neural Networks, Barceló et al. ICLR 2020) has been a major factor in forming today’s understanding of MPGNNs.

>Q5 Theorem 3 is proven using two CSL graphs (though with 16 nodes). Do you have an intuition why in Table 1 the CSL results for EB-GNN do not improve over MPNN+C3?

The graphs from Theorem 3 are not actually CSL graphs. Indeed, they are 6-regular while CSL graphs are 4-regular (in CSL graphs, there is just 1 skip-link length while each graph from Theorem 3 has 2). Thus, intuitively, CSL graphs are not sufficiently complex to distinguish MPNN+C3 from EB-GNN, while a small modification as in Theorem 3 already separates EB-GNN even from NC-1WL (that captures MPNN+C3).

comment.value:
> W1 The novelty is limited. The authors propose only a slight alteration of the NC-1WL method.

We would like to point out that in addition to the method itself, we provide foundational results about its expressivity: we present a tight first-order logic characterization (Theorem 3), as well as distinguishability results based on homomorphism counts (Theorem 4), which are highly nontrivial to obtain. Furthermore, we provide comparisons with 1WL, NC-1WL and 2WL. Analogous foundational results for the NC-1WL test are absent in the literature.

> W2, W3 The expressivity discussion is limited. While the authors formulate some lower bound (Thm.5), the experimental results on e.g. BREC are not put into perspective. It is unclear what the increased expressivity can be actually attributed to. It is unclear what the role of the first-order-logic formulation is. I don't see any implications of this.

Thank you for suggesting relating experimental results on BREC with our theoretical expressivity results. Results on BREC indeed can be put into a wider theoretical perspective, and we elaborate more on that in the answer to your Question 4.

> W4 While the authors' approach is based on NC-1WL, it is never compared to in Section 6. Table 1 contains only very few competitor methods. 

Thank you for pointing this out. Unfortunately, the code for NC-GNN is not publicly available and the authors did not reply to our email. Thus, we re-implemented NC-GNN ourselves and have run an additional benchmark to compare the predictive performance of NC1-GNN with our EB-GNN. This benchmark covers CSL, BREC, QMD and MalNet-Tiny; we did not perform experiments on QM9 as a fair evaluation on this dataset would have taken too long for the rebuttal period. For all datasets, we set and tune hyperparameters exactly as for EB-GNN.

On synthetic datasets (see Table 1), we outperform NC-GNN in two out of five categories and tie it in the remaining two. Notably, on extension graphs EB-GNN solves 60 instances while NC-GNN solves 0, highlighting our empirical increase in expressivity.

The results for QMD can be found in Table 3 of our updated paper. In summary, even with the added NC1-GNN baseline, EB-GNN remains the best performing model in 6 / 8 tasks (in the other tasks the best model is an MPNN). On the four edge-level tasks, EB-GNN outperforms NC-GNN by 8,5% on average and up to 13,9%. The results for MalNet-Tiny can be found in Table 2:  EB-GNN remains the best performing model on this dataset with NC-GNN reaching third place (out of seven) demonstrating the empirical strength of edge-based GNNs.

>W5  It would be interesting to compare to the methods from Table 4 on synthetic datasets as well.

Thank you for the suggestion. We have added entries to Table 1 for all models from Table 4 with available synthetic dataset results, as well as for NC-GNN, adding a total of four new entries.

>W6 Theorem 3 is incomplete. The second sentence is not a consequence of the first.

Thank you for pointing out this imprecission. Indeed, the second sentence is the consequence of the first one sentence together with the directly preceding Proposition 2. In the revised paper, we have merged Proposition 2 into the previous Theorem 3 and clarified the language.

>W7 Lines 178-181 need to be explained in more detail. While the Chiba&Nishizeki algorithm is even mentioned in the abstract, it is never discussed. I would recommend to at least mention what the arboricity is. Otherwise, Proposition 1 is not understandable.

Thank you for this note, we have added the definition of arboricity to the main text and a detailed discussion of the relationship between the Chiba–Nishizeki algorithm and our architecture to Appendix A.

Thank you for your detailed response to my comments. I appreciate the effort you've put into addressing my questions and remarks. I will raise my score in recognition of your clarifications. 

Nonetheless, I still believe that the overall contribution of the paper remains relatively modest. While the main results are certainly interesting (e.g. Thm 4 ), I believe they do not offer a sufficiently significant or novel advancement to the GNN community. Therefore, I still cannot fully recommend acceptance of the paper.

summary.value: This paper proposes edge-based WL (EB-1WL) test which has been proved to be strictly power than 1-WL test,  NC-WL-test but less than 2-WL test. Based on the proposed edge-based WL test, edge-based GNN (EB-GNN) is builted to achieve EB-1WL test.

strengths.value:
1. It is interesting to see a newly proposed WL test algorithm that demonstrates stronger expressive power than existing WL tests, while still maintaining reasonable computational efficiency.

2. The writing and organization of the paper are clear and easy to follow.

weaknesses.value:
1. Although the authors claim that the proposed method is more powerful than NC-1WL, the experimental results of NC-GNN and its efficiency are not included as a baseline in the experiments.
In addition, the experimental section lacks evaluations on large-scale graph datasets such as COLLAB, which would better demonstrate the efficiency and scalability of the model. 
It would also be helpful to report the GPU memory usage of each model to provide a more complete comparison of computational cost.

2. A comparison between the proposed EB-1WL test and other WL variants beyond NC-1WL is not discussed. For instance, 
	the baseline model 5-ℓGIN introduces the r-ℓWL test—what is the relationship between this and EB-1WL? 
	Moreover, is EB-1WL theoretically or empirically more powerful, leading to better performance on the QM9 dataset?

On the four edge-level tasks, EB-GNN outperforms NC-GNN by 8,5% on average and up to 13,9%. > In addition, the experimental section lacks evaluations on large-scale graph datasets such as COLLAB, which would better demonstrate the efficiency and scalability of the model. 

We would like to point out that our evaluation covers datasets that are substantially larger than COLLAB. Concretely, COLLAB consists of 5000 graphs with on average 75 nodes. We cannot provide precise GPU memory measurements within the rebuttal timeframe. Memory usage depends heavily on implementation details and experimental settings (e.g., batch size), so accurately comparing models would require re-implementing the GNNs in our framework, which is not feasible. For context, we note that our EB-GNN trains on a single consumer-grade GPU (NVIDIA RTX 3080 with 10 GB RAM), demonstrating that it is not particularly memory-intensive.

summary.value:
The authors propose the EB-1WL test for graph isomorphism, from which they define EB GNNs, motivated by a triangle counting algorithm in the TCS literature. 
They show that the EB-1WL test is more expressive compared to 1-WL, and study its logical expressiveness and hormorphism counting power. 

For the logical part, they characterize the power in terms of the so-called clique-based finite-variable fragments (Theorem 4).  For the homomorphism count, they show that EB GNN can distinguish chordal graphs of treewidth two, which is something between 1-WL and 2-WL  (Theorem 5)


Moreover, they show that the proposed method, EB GNN, needs only linear time and memory for specific graph tasks. 
Indeed, if some parameter called the absorbcity of the graph is bounded, then each iteration of their algorithm only runs in almost linear time in the number of edges. 
The method is formulated in Equations 1-4. They conclude the paper with supporting experiments.

strengths.value:
- The new method based on message passing on edges, with provable expressivity, is of potential interest to the graph ML community 

- The paper is well-written and clean

weaknesses.value: - The computation complexity reduction is restricted to some assumptions. And it is not clear whether those assumptions will break the symmetry/power of the method or not.

questions.value:
This is an interesting, well-written paper on graph ML. The authors introduced EB GNNs, based a novel idea on message passing on edges. The authors supported the introduction of their method by proving that it's better than 1-WL in terms of expressive power, as well as showing (theoretically) how it can count homomorphisms and how it can express logical formulae for graphs. They are also supported by experiments. 

I have a number of questions/comments:

 - Line 178: 'If we iterate..." The question i,s why are you allowed to do this? Did this keep the permutation invariance, and will it break it? If you only do the iteration over the low-degree nodes, then do you still get the full expressivity (proven in the paper)? This is a main weakness of the paper. I ask the authors to provide more explanation on this.

- The improvement in time complexity is exciting; however, there are also some lower bounds that GNNs cannot break. If the average degree of the graph is small, then one cannot count subgraphs in linear time (I found it here [1], but there might be other theoretical papers you can find on the web, too). So please specify exactly when the time complexity of your method is small. If $m$ is of order $n^2$ (dense graph), then can't you just do 2 or higher order WL? If $m$ is of order $n$ (sparse graph), then the average degree is of course $O(1)$, so you can just search over neighborhoods (similar to [1]) and you are probably fine?


I feel my concern is fully addressed if you can explain more and compare with known TCS complexity bounds. I provided one reference just for instance, but please do search, as there might be other ones. 






[1] Tahmasebi, Behrooz, Derek Lim, and Stefanie Jegelka. "The power of recursion in graph neural networks for counting substructures." In International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics, pp. 11023-11042. PMLR, 2023.


---

Overall, this is an interesting paper and I'm happy to increase my score if the authors provide answers to my concerns.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission4539 by Reviewer 3SPZ

comment.value:
Thank you for reviewing our paper and for engaging in the rebuttal.

> Line 178: 'If we iterate..." The question is why are you allowed to do this? Did this keep the permutation invariance, and will it break it? If you only do the iteration over the low-degree nodes, then do you still get the full expressivity (proven in the paper)? This is a main weakness of the paper. I ask the authors to provide more explanation on this.

We thank the reviewer for pointing this out and will clarify the text. Concretely, we stress that our construction enumerates all triangles and includes all of them in the corresponding summations (such as Equation (3)). The “iterate over the lower-degree endpoint” phrasing is not a restriction on which triangles are considered, but only an implementation detail of the Chiba–Nishizeki triangle enumeration algorithm to optimize its efficiency. Thus, every triangle $(u,v,w)$ still contributes to the aggregated messages. Since the aggregations in EB-1WL/EB-GNN are defined via permutation-invariant functions, the order in which we enumerate neighbors or triangles does not affect the result, and therefore does not impact permutation invariance or the expressivity guarantees proved in the paper. We made this more explicit in the revised paper and added a reference to the newly added Appendix A, where we now give a more detailed description of the Chiba–Nishizeki algorithm, its role in our complexity analysis and how it inspired our architecture.

> The improvement in time complexity is exciting; however, there are also some lower bounds that GNNs cannot break. If the average degree of the graph is small, then one cannot count subgraphs in linear time (I found it here [1], but there might be other theoretical papers you can find on the web, too). So please specify exactly when the time complexity of your method is small. If m is of order n^2 (dense graph), then can't you just do 2 or higher order WL? If m is of order n (sparse graph), then the average degree is of course O(1), so you can just search over neighborhoods (similar to [1]) and you are probably fine?

We thank the reviewer for raising this point and will clarify the complexity discussion accordingly. Our preprocessing relies on the Chiba–Nishizeki algorithm, which enumerates all triangles in time $O(\alpha m)$, where $\alpha$ is the arboricity. As we now highlight in Appendix A, this running time is conditionally optimal under standard conjectures from the fine-grained complexity theory community (see references [A] and [B] below), so a substantially faster triangle enumeration algorithm would refute these assumptions.

The lower bounds in [1] concern general subgraph counting on bounded average-degree graphs and do not contradict our guarantees: even when the average degree is $O(1)$, the arboricity can still be as large as $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$. We explicitly give such an example in Appendix A (a path on $n-\sqrt{n}$ nodes attached to a clique on $\sqrt{n}$ nodes), which has average degree $O(1)$ but arboricity $\Theta(\sqrt{n})$. In such a case, the Chiba–Nishizeki algorithm needs time $O(n^{1.5})$ (indeed, this is optimal since it has to output $\Theta(n^{1.5})$ triangles). Moreover, “just searching over neighborhoods” can be substantially worse than our $O(\alpha m)$ bound: for instance, a star-like graph has average degree $O(1)$ and arboricity $O(1)$, but a naïve neighborhood-based triangle search would examine $\Theta(n^2)$ pairs of neighbors at the hub, whereas Chiba–Nishizeki runs in $O(m)$ time on such graphs.

We agree that when $m = \Omega(n^2)$ (very dense graphs), 2WL or higher-order WL becomes comparable in running time, and one could in principle use these instead of EB-GNN. Our contribution is primarily targeted at the practically relevant regime where graphs are sparse and have low arboricity, which is well documented both in the algorithms literature and empirically (e.g., Eppstein et al., 2013, footnote 1 on page 2 of our submission, and our datasets in Section 6). We will make these regimes explicit in the main text of the final version and point to Appendix A for the detailed discussion of arboricity, conditional optimality, and concrete examples.

[A] Tsvi Kopelowitz, Seth Pettie, Ely Porat: Higher Lower Bounds from the 3SUM Conjecture. SODA 2016: 1272-1287
[B] Virginia Vassilevska Williams, Yinzhan Xu: Monochromatic Triangles, Triangle Listing and APSP. FOCS 2020: 786-797

The biggest issue is that the proposed method is not new. 

1. The local-neighbor based extension is a special case of https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.01543
2. Using existing edges as restricted 2-tuple is a special case of https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.09521. See figure 1 and appendix A.12. Notice that in figure 1, the equation (1) (2) (3) (4) corresponds to the connection shown in solid line and yellow nodes. The only difference, is that this paper changes the study from set to tuple, which actually is designed to be removed by the paper. See section 3.2 for the discussion of moving from tuple to set. While I do agree that order somehow has certain expressivity, but the paper is not interesting given the proof does not prove the importance of using tuple instead of set. In general, while being slightly different, I think the small modification does not worth a paper unless the author proof the expressivity improvement. (Notice that the computation cost should be the same) 

In general, I feel that the author lacks significant amount of literature review, especially regarding to efficient higher-order GNNs, and also subgraph GNNs. Papers from Haggai Maron, Bohang Zhang, Muhan Zhang, and others expressivity researchers are necessary to review and study.

comment.value:
Thank you for reviewing our paper and for engaging in the rebuttal.

> The local-neighbor based extension is a special case of https://arxiv.org/pdf/1904.01543

If we understand the reviewer’s comments correctly, this refers to the fact that in our color refinement update (Equations (2) and (4) in our paper) we quantify over the neighbors of a vertex, and $\delta$-k-LWL also quantifies over each component vertex’s neighbors. 

While this might look similar at first sight, they are in fact conceptually and technically quite different. We illustrate this with a 2-hop path as a simple example graph:
a — b — c

The $\delta$-2-WL update for (a,b) would update based on the pair of multisets $\\{C(a,x) \mid x \in N(b)\\}$ and $\\{C(x,c) \mid x \in N(a)\\}$, where C is the coloring at the previous layer. Note that both of these multisets are $\\{C(a,c)\\}$. That is, we replace each component with all of its neighbors, i.e., a classic $k$-WL style update but limited to local neighborhoods.

The seemingly similar part of our update (i.e., only Equations (2) and (4), ignoring Equation (3)) would update based on $\\{C(a,x) \mid x \in N(a) \\}$ (Equation (2)) and $\\{ C(b,x) \mid x \in N(b) \\}$ (Equation (4)). Thus, we obtain the differing multisets $\\{C(a,b)\\}$ and $\\{C(b,c)\\}$, i.e., the update is based on the edges incident to edge $(a,b)$ (and the edge itself).

Notably, while the linked paper is motivated by exploiting sparseness, they achieve $\Theta(n^2 d)$ runtime for a round of $\delta$-2-LWL, where $d$ is the maximum degree of the graph. This is notably slower compared to our per-layer runtime of $O(\alpha m)$, where in sparse graphs we have $m \ll n^2$ and $\alpha \ll d$.

We hope this example clarifies that the two approaches are conceptually quite far apart, despite their apparent syntactic closeness. We have added an extended discussion about this interesting contrast between the two approaches in Appendix D.

> Using existing edges as restricted 2-tuple is a special case of https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.09521 [...]

Thank you for pointing out this paper. We argue that our architecture cannot be realized as a special case of any computationally efficient test in this framework: any $(k,c)(≤)$-SetWL instance that is at least as expressive as our method necessarily operates on higher-order tuples and thus incurs substantially larger space requirements, whereas our architecture is explicitly designed for the low-space/low-time regime.
Specifically, the paper defines a family of $(k,c)(\leq)$-SetWL tests. For $k = 2$, this is a restricted version of the non-folklore 2WL, equivalent to the 1WL test, while our architecture is strictly more powerful than the 1WL-test. Furthermore, for $k=3$, the $(3,1)(\leq)$-SetWL test assigns colors to all 3-subsets of nodes with at most 1 connected component in the induced subgraphs – that is to all triangles and paths of length 2. Thus, the memory requirements for this test are substantially more demanding than the space and time complexity of our architecture. As a concrete example, consider a star graph with $n$ nodes. Our architecture takes time and space linear in $n$, because the arboricity of this graph is 1. On the other hand, $(3,1)(\leq)$-SetWL requires memory of order $\Theta(n^2)$ as there are $\Theta(n^2)$ paths of length 2.
We therefore firmly disagree with the claim that this prior work affects our claimed contributions: they exhibit worse scaling behaviour in terms of layer time complexity (especially in sparse graphs), and they do not present any clear theoretical characterisation of their expressive power along the lines of Theorem 4 and Theorem 5.

We added a discussion of this paper into the revised version, and we further extended our related work section.

We thank the reviewers for their interest and their feedback. We believe the questions have helped us to substantially improve the submission in terms of both clarity and content. We have uploaded a revision of the paper, in which we made the changes detailed below.

We have extended our experiments, adding an experimental comparison to the related NC1-GNNs. Overall, EB-GNN is consistently stronger than NC1-GNN: it solves 60 extension-graph instances where NC1-GNN solves none, achieves up to 13.9% higher accuracy on edge-level QMD tasks, and is the best-performing model on MalNet-Tiny and on 6 of the 8 QMD tasks (on the remaining two, NC1-GNN is slightly better, but a simple MPNN already outperforms both). We note that the original implementation for NC1-GNN was not available to us and our results are based on our reimplementation according to their paper.

Furthermore, we have clarified why we firmly disagree with the claim that linked prior work affects our claimed contributions. In short, the references pointed out by the reviewers exhibit substantially worse scaling behavior in terms of layer time complexity (especially in sparse graphs), and they do not present any clear theoretical characterization of their expressive power along the lines of our Theorem 4 and Theorem 5. We invite the reviewers to see our response to Reviewer veqN for further details.

Additionally, we have ​​clarified the role of the arboricity and how the Chiba–Nishizeki algorithm inspired our architecture (see the new Appendix A), the relationship to theoretical results on pattern counting, and we have extended the related work to incorporate the references pointed out by the reviewers, as well as other additional references.

comment.value:
We provide a summary of the reviewers’ main concerns and how we have addressed them.

**Novelty:** Two reviewers (L5Lp, veqN) claimed that our results have limited novelty when compared to NC-1-WL, $\\delta$-$k$-WL or $(k, c)(\\leq)$-SETWL. We showed in the rebuttal that either our architecture is more expressive (compared to NC-1-WL) or substantially more computationally efficient (compared to $\\delta$-$k$-WL and $(k,c)(\\leq)$-SETWL). More specifically, the comparison is as follows:
- NC-1-WL: Our architecture is more expressive (Theorem 2) and performs better empirically (Table 1, 2 and 3). Furthermore, we provide a tight expressivity characterization of our architecture in terms of homomorphism counts and first-order logic. In particular, this allows us to also give us upper bounds of the expressivity of NC-1-WL: every property that cannot be distinguished based on our characterization is also not distinguishable by NC-1-WL.  
- $\\delta$-$k$-WL: We believe this comparison may be the result of the reviewer misreading something. The aggregation method here is substantially different both conceptually and technically (see our reply to Reviewer veqN). Notably, while this architecture is motivated by exploiting sparseness, it only achieves $\Theta(n^2 d)$ runtime for a round of $\delta$-2-LWL, where $d$ is the maximum degree of the graph. This is notably slower compared to our per-layer runtime of $O(\alpha m)$, where in sparse graphs we have $m \ll n^2$ and $\alpha \ll d$.  
- $(k, c)(\\leq)$-SETWL: When setting $k = 2$ this architecture does compute edge embeddings. However, this does not achieve expressivity beyond 1-WL for $k=2$. Hence $k = 3$ is required to achieve expressivity comparable to our approach, at which point this architecture computes embeddings for all 3-sets of nodes which requires substantially more memory and runtime than our architecture. Additionally, in contrast to key parts of our submission, no theoretical characterisations are provided in that paper.

**Missing Baselines:** Two reviewers (L5Lp, i4hW) have asked for empirical comparisons to NC-1-WL. We have evaluated the requested GNN on the CSL, BREC, QMD and MalNetTiny datasets. For real-world datasets, we outperform NC-1-WL on 6 / 8 tasks on QMD and on MalNetTiny. On synthetic datasets, we outperform NC-GNN in two out of five categories and tie it in the remaining two. Notably, on extension graphs EB-GNN solves 60 instances while NC-GNN solves 0, highlighting our empirical increase in expressivity. Please see our reply to Reviewer i4hW for more details.

display_title: Meta Review of Submission4539 by Area Chair Dpby

summary.value: This paper proposes EB-1WL, an extension of the WL test, and a corresponding architecture (EB-GNN) that uses triangle-based message passing to achieve improved expressivity over 1-WL (and less than 2-WL). Reviewers appreciate the paper's clear writing and technical care in formalism (veqN, 3SPZ), and theoretical characterizations via FOL and homomorphism counting that are potentially valuable to the expressivity literature (3SPZ, veqN), and competitive empirical performance with good efficiency (i4hW, L5Lp). However, reviewers raised multiple points of concern: limited perceived novelty relative to prior NC-1WL / higher-order WL variants (veqN, L5Lp), some concerns about whether expressivity gains are sizeable enough to justify a new framework, especially caveated on that complexity advantages rely on specific regimes (e.g. low arboricity) which have some unclear scope/assumption (3SPZ). While authors added missing baselines and clarifications in rebuttal, reviewers were unconvinced that the contribution was a step function size-able enough to warrant acceptance at this time.  Moreover, the initial ratings are not strong and there is limited confidence that the clarifications during rebuttal period would have pushed this paper over the line.  I encourage the authors to further sharpen the novelty claims and better position the work relative to the contending architectures and works the reviewers pointed out.
